channel.description: Recent content in Ai_assistant on Best of AI

item.title: Baidu ERNIE
item.description:
ERNIE, which stands for Enhanced Representation through Knowledge Integration, is Baidu’s answer to ChatGPT. The consumer chatbot answers questions, writes and edits text, generates images, and handles tasks in Chinese and other languages, and it is built into Baidu’s search engine and apps. It benefits from Baidu’s knowledge graph and search data, and is a major option for Chinese-language users.

For developers and companies, Baidu offers ERNIE models through its Qianfan cloud platform, with APIs, fine-tuning, and tools for building AI applications. The company has released versions of its models with open weights, which lets developers run them independently. The models support multimodal inputs and reasoning, and are used in enterprise products, cloud services, and Baidu’s autonomous driving and other businesses.

item.title: Dia
item.description:
Dia puts an AI assistant at the center of web browsing. The address bar accepts both web addresses and questions, so you can search, ask about the page you are viewing, or have the assistant work across several open tabs, such as comparing products or summarizing a set of articles. It can draft writing in context and pull from what you have open.

The browser keeps familiar elements such as tabs and extensions, but adds features that use browsing history and open pages as context, with options for custom skills that package repeated prompts. It focuses on helping with everyday tasks like research, email drafts, and shopping comparisons.

item.title: Elasticsearch
item.description: Elasticsearch stores documents as JSON and indexes them so searches come back in milliseconds, even across billions of records. It began as a full-text search engine for things like product catalogs and website search, and it is also used heavily for logs, metrics, and security data. It is the core of the Elastic Stack, which adds Kibana for dashboards, and ingestion tools for getting data in. Companies use it wherever they need to search or aggregate a large volume of text-heavy data quickly.

item.title: Meilisearch
item.description:
Meilisearch focuses on delivering relevant results quickly with little configuration. Developers send their documents to it through a simple API, and it returns ranked results as the user types, with typo tolerance, synonyms, filtering, and sorting working out of the box. That makes it popular for adding search to a store or a knowledge base.

Newer features address AI. Hybrid search combines keyword matching with vector similarity, so a query can find results by meaning as well as exact words, and it can connect to embedding models. Teams can host Meilisearch themselves, since it is open source, or use the company’s managed cloud.

item.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot
item.description: Microsoft 365 Copilot is the business version of Microsoft’s AI, and its main advantage is context. It can see your files, emails, calendar, chats, and meetings through Microsoft Graph, within the permissions you already have. In Word it drafts and rewrites documents based on other files, in Outlook it summarizes long threads and drafts replies, and in Teams it recaps meetings, lists decisions, and answers questions about what was discussed. PowerPoint can build a deck from a document, and Excel can explain formulas and analyze data with plain-language prompts.

item.title: MURAL
item.description:
MURAL gives distributed teams a shared canvas. Participants add sticky notes, diagrams, images, and text to a large board at the same time, and facilitators run sessions with tools such as timers, private mode for individual thinking, voting, and guided agendas. A big library of templates covers retros, roadmaps, design sprints, and strategy exercises.

AI assists with the messy part of workshops, which is making sense of dozens of notes. It can group sticky notes by theme, summarize a board, and generate ideas to get a session started. Integrations with Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Jira, and Slack connect boards to the tools where work gets done.

item.title: Nomi
item.description:
Nomi lets users build a personal AI companion. You choose a name, appearance, personality traits, and backstory, then chat by text or voice. The app emphasizes memory, so the character recalls details you shared in earlier conversations and builds a continuing relationship, which is what many users value about it.

Relationship type is configurable, and group chats and shared experiences add variety. Users can see the companion’s interests and send images, and the creators have promoted the idea of an emotionally rich AI that grows with the user. The app runs on mobile and web.

item.title: Typesense
item.description:
Typesense is built for instant search experiences, like the results that appear as a user types in a store or documentation site. It keeps its index in memory for speed, handles typos by default, and supports filtering, faceting, sorting, and grouping. Its API is simple, and client libraries exist for popular languages.

It also supports modern retrieval needs. Vector search lets applications find results by meaning using embeddings, and hybrid search combines that with keyword matching. Built-in features can generate embeddings, and a conversational search mode answers questions using retrieved documents. Developers can run Typesense on their own servers or use Typesense Cloud.

item.title: TypingMind
item.description:
TypingMind is a front end for AI models. A user supplies API keys, and gets a clean chat app with conversation folders, prompt libraries, and tools. Pay-per-use API pricing can be cheaper than several subscriptions, especially for light users.

Features include support for multiple models in one place, custom assistants, plugins, and knowledge uploads, and teams can share setups with controlled access. It is a paid product with a one-time or subscription license depending on the plan.

item.title: Ando
item.description:
Ando rethinks team chat for a workplace where software agents work next to people. In most chat tools, AI is an add-on bot. In Ando, agents have identities, inboxes, and permissions, and they can join channels, read ongoing conversations, and message teammates, just like human members.

The product has the familiar parts of a messaging platform, including channels, direct messages, group conversations, and calls. The difference is how agents are treated: a person can assign work to an agent in a thread, and the agent can respond, ask questions, and report back. Teams can bring agents built on different models.

item.title: Claude Docs
item.description:
Claude Docs brings document writing into the chat. Instead of copying an answer from a conversation into another app, you ask Claude to draft a report, memo, or plan, and it appears as a document you can edit beside the conversation. You can revise it by typing changes directly or by asking Claude to rework sections.

Documents are stored in the Artifacts tab, so they are easy to find later and update across sessions. When the draft is ready, it can be exported to common formats such as Word, PDF, Google Docs, or Markdown. The tool handles headings, lists, and tables, and it works with files and context shared in the conversation.

item.title: Google CC
item.description:
CC acts like a morning assistant. Each day it sends an email, called Your Day Ahead, that pulls together calendar events, important messages, bills, and documents relevant to the day. You reply to the email to ask for changes, such as adding an event or digging into a topic, and CC acts on it.

It connects to a user’s Gmail, Calendar, and Drive and can also use the web for context. Because it works through email, there is no new app to learn. Google has expanded the experiment to support shared use by members of a household, with each person connecting their own accounts.

item.title: Zetik
item.description:
Zetik is a personal research assistant. A user picks topics, and the system monitors many source types, ranks what matters, and delivers a concise brief, so they stay informed without scanning feeds. It aims to surface signal across places that are hard to follow manually.

This suits founders, investors, and researchers who track fast-moving fields. Summaries need to link back to sources, and personalization improves as the tool learns what the user finds relevant.

item.title: Algolia AI Search
item.description:
Algolia is a hosted search service known for speed. Developers send it their data, such as products, articles, or help center pages, and use its APIs and UI libraries to add search that responds as the user types, with typo tolerance, filters, and facets. Many e-commerce and media sites use it.

Its AI search layer extends that with newer methods. Hybrid search blends keyword matching with vector similarity so queries find results by meaning, and tools can personalize ranking from user behavior. Merchandisers can adjust relevance with business rules without code, and the platform supports retrieval for conversational and agent experiences, where an AI model answers using the retrieved content.

item.title: DeepSeek
item.description: DeepSeek is an AI research company based in China whose models are released with their weights open, so anyone can download, run, and fine-tune them. Its general-purpose models handle chat, writing, and coding, and its reasoning models work through a problem step by step before answering. What got the industry’s attention was efficiency: DeepSeek’s models perform near the best closed systems on many math and coding benchmarks while being far cheaper to train and serve. Its technical papers, which describe how it did this, are widely read by other labs.

item.title: DeepSeek Chat
item.description:
DeepSeek Chat offers consumer access to DeepSeek’s language models. Users ask questions, draft text, write code, and work through math and logic, and a mode shows the model’s step-by-step reasoning before it gives an answer. It supports uploading files and searching the web.

DeepSeek drew wide attention when its models matched strong Western systems at much lower reported training cost, and it released the model weights openly, which let others run and study them. The chat app was one of the most downloaded in many countries soon after it launched.

item.title: Elastic AI Assistant
item.description:
Elastic AI Assistant is built into the Elastic stack, which many companies use for search, logs, and security monitoring. Users ask questions in plain language, such as what caused a spike in errors or what an alert means, and the assistant queries the data, explains findings, and suggests next steps.

For security teams, it helps triage alerts, write queries, and summarize incidents using the organization’s own data. For observability, it assists with investigating logs and metrics. Retrieval from indexed content grounds answers in real information, and administrators choose which language model provider to connect.

item.title: Gemini Pro
item.description: Gemini Pro refers to the mid-sized models in Google’s Gemini family, positioned between the smaller, cheaper Flash models and the heaviest reasoning options. Google’s naming moves with each generation, but the idea stays the same: Pro is the version intended for demanding everyday work without the cost or delay of the very largest model. Gemini was designed from the start to take in several types of input at once, so the same model reads text, looks at images, listens to audio, and watches video rather than handing those jobs to separate systems.

item.title: Mistral
item.description: Mistral is Europe’s best-known frontier AI lab. It first drew attention by releasing compact open-weight models that matched or beat larger ones, and it has continued to release models in several sizes for chat, coding, reasoning, and vision. Some are free to download under permissive licenses, while its strongest models are offered through its API and Le Chat. Developers like that it gives them the choice to run models on their own hardware.

item.title: Qwen Studio
item.description:
Qwen Studio is the consumer-facing way to use Alibaba’s Qwen models. Users chat with the assistant, search the web, upload documents and images for analysis, write code, and generate pictures and video. A mode shows the model’s reasoning for harder problems.

The Qwen family is notable for open-weight releases that developers can download and run, so Qwen Studio doubles as a showcase of what those models can do. It supports many languages, with strong coverage of Chinese and English.

item.title: Submit AI Tools
item.description:
Submit AI Tools collects AI products in a searchable list. Visitors browse by category, read short descriptions, and click through to the tools. Makers submit listings to get discovered.

As with other directories, coverage depends on submissions and editorial review, so details can be incomplete or out of date. It works best as one of several places to scan.

The site is free. Check each tool’s own site for pricing and privacy information. Similar resources include Futurepedia, There’s An AI For That, Aixploria, OpenTools, and Best of AI. Submit AI Tools suits people browsing for AI products.

item.title: AIPRM
item.description:
AIPRM saves people from writing prompts from scratch. Its browser extension adds a prompt library to the ChatGPT interface, organized by topic such as SEO, sales, customer support, productivity, and writing. You pick a prompt template, fill in details like your topic or audience, and it sends a detailed, well-structured instruction to the AI. Users can also create, save, and share their own prompts.

The library grew from community contributions, which means quality varies, though ratings and usage counts help identify useful ones. Paid plans add private prompts, team sharing, and prompt management for organizations, plus integrations with other AI tools. It is popular with marketers and SEO professionals who run the same kinds of tasks repeatedly, such as keyword clustering or content briefs.

item.title: Landbot
item.description:
Landbot lets non-developers design conversations visually. A user drags blocks onto a canvas to ask questions, branch based on answers, and connect to other tools, then publishes the flow on a website, a landing page, or WhatsApp. The conversational format often gets more responses than a plain form.

AI features add the ability to answer free-text questions from a knowledge base and to build flows from a description. Integrations send leads to CRMs and spreadsheets, and handoff routes complex chats to human agents. Templates cover lead generation, support, and onboarding.

item.title: Perplexity Pro
item.description:
Perplexity is an answer engine that searches the web and writes cited responses. The Pro tier raises limits on advanced searches and lets users choose among models, including Perplexity’s own and leading models from other labs, for harder questions.

Pro adds tools for research: upload and analyze documents, longer and more detailed searches, image generation, and access to deeper research modes that produce reports. Spaces let users organize topics and collaborate, and an API credit is sometimes included.

item.title: Andi
item.description:
Andi is a search engine for people who find link lists cluttered. You ask a question, and it returns a short answer with cited sources, plus links you can open. The idea is to combine the answering ability of a language model with the freshness of the web.

Privacy and design are part of the pitch. Andi has said it does not rely on advertising or sell user data, and the interface is clean, with options to refine a query and explore related questions. It is one of several startups, along with Perplexity, You.com, and Phind, that took on the conventional search model.

item.title: Arc Browser
item.description: Arc reimagined the browser. Instead of a row of tabs across the top, it uses a vertical sidebar where tabs are grouped into spaces, such as work and personal, each with its own pinned items and theme. Tabs that you do not use are archived automatically, and features like split view, boosts for customizing websites, and easels for collecting ideas made it a favorite of power users and designers. It is built on Chromium, so most Chrome extensions work.

item.title: Asana
item.description: Asana organizes work as tasks inside projects. Each task has an owner, a due date, and a place in a larger plan, and the same project can be viewed as a list, a kanban board, a timeline, or a calendar. Teams use it for campaign planning, product launches, client work, and operations requests, anywhere several people need to see who is doing what and by when. Portfolios and Goals roll individual projects up into a view managers can read without opening every one.

item.title: Bing Chat
item.description: Bing Chat was Microsoft’s first big move into AI-assisted search. It put a conversational assistant next to the Bing search box, so you could ask a question and get a written answer with links to sources instead of scanning a page of results. Microsoft later renamed and expanded it as Copilot, and the assistant now works across the web, in the Edge browser, in Windows, and in standalone mobile and desktop apps.

item.title: Brave Leo
item.description: Leo sits in the browser’s sidebar and works with whatever page you are viewing. You can ask it to summarize an article or a long video transcript, explain a technical passage, extract key points from a PDF, or answer questions about the content, without copying text into a separate chatbot. It can also help write or rewrite text, translate, brainstorm, and answer general questions, with the option of using the web for current information.

item.title: ChatGPT
item.description: ChatGPT is a chat interface to OpenAI’s language models. You type or speak a request and it answers in plain language, whether that means drafting an email, explaining a concept, debugging a function, or summarizing a long PDF. It can take images and files as input and generate images in return. For many people it is the first AI tool they ever used, and that familiarity is a big part of why it remains the default comparison for every other assistant.

item.title: Claude
item.description: Claude is the AI assistant from Anthropic, a company that focuses on AI safety research. It comes in a few model tiers, with smaller and faster models for quick tasks and larger ones for harder reasoning and coding. People tend to pick it for writing that sounds less formulaic, careful reading of long documents, and code. It is also more willing than some competitors to say it is unsure or to disagree with you, which some users value and others find less accommodating.

item.title: Clickup
item.description: ClickUp tries to be a single home for everything a team does. At its center are tasks that can be shown as lists, boards, calendars, Gantt charts, or timelines, and each task can have subtasks, custom fields, dependencies, and checklists. Around that sit docs, wikis, whiteboards, forms, dashboards, goals, and built-in chat. Teams use it for software sprints, marketing calendars, client projects, and operations, and the same workspace can be shaped differently for each department.

item.title: Coda AI
item.description:
Coda reimagines the document as something that can behave like an app. A Coda doc can contain text, tables, buttons, and automations, so a team can build a project tracker, a wiki, a CRM, or a planning tool in the same document where they write. Formulas, similar to those in spreadsheets, connect data across the doc, and Packs integrate with outside services such as Slack, Jira, and Google Calendar.

AI features run through the platform. Coda AI can summarize documents, draft text, fill table columns with generated content, categorize and extract information, and answer questions about the contents of a doc. AI blocks and agents can be placed in workflows to automate tasks. The company joined Grammarly, which has taken the name Superhuman, and its tools are being combined with Grammarly’s writing assistant and the Superhuman email app.

item.title: Devv.ai
item.description: Devv.ai was built as a search tool for programmers, positioned between a traditional search engine and a chatbot. You ask a technical question, such as how to configure a library or why an error occurs, and it searches documentation, GitHub repositories, and developer discussions and then writes an answer with sources. Linking to sources helps you verify the answer, which matters because chatbots can invent APIs or settings that do not exist.

item.title: Exa AI
item.description: Exa, formerly Metaphor, rethinks search for machines instead of people. Where a traditional engine matches keywords, Exa uses neural embeddings to find pages that are semantically similar to a query, even when they do not share words. You can search with natural-language descriptions, such as a list of startups building a specific kind of robot, and it returns results that match the idea. It can also take a link and find similar pages.

item.title: Gemini
item.description: Gemini is Google’s family of AI models and the assistant built on top of them. You can use it in the standalone Gemini app and website, but it also shows up inside the products many people already use: it can help draft emails in Gmail, rewrite text in Docs, summarize files in Drive, and answer questions on Android phones. If most of your work and personal life already runs on a Google account, that integration is the main reason to choose Gemini over another assistant.

item.title: Gemini Advanced
item.description:
Gemini Advanced was Google’s answer to ChatGPT Plus. When Google rebranded Bard as Gemini, it introduced Advanced as a subscription, sold through Google One, that gave access to its strongest model, longer conversations, and features like file uploads and integration with Gmail and Docs. It also bundled extra Google One storage, which made it attractive to people already paying for cloud storage.

Google later reorganized the plans. Gemini Advanced’s features moved into Google AI Pro, and a higher tier called Google AI Ultra provides the most advanced models, agent features, and generous limits for heavy users. The plans include perks such as video generation, deeper research tools, and integrations with Workspace apps, and the exact lineup changes with each product update.

item.title: Gemini in Workspace
item.description:
Gemini in Workspace brings Google’s models into the apps people use at work. In Gmail, it drafts replies and summarizes long threads. In Docs, it writes, rewrites, and proofreads, and can pull in information from files and email. In Sheets, it helps create formulas, tables, and analysis. In Slides, it generates slides and images, and in Meet it takes notes and summarizes.

A side panel gives a chat assistant that can search across a user’s Drive, Gmail, and Calendar, and answer questions using that content. Organizations can control access, and Google states that business data is not used to train models without permission. Newer features include agents and tools such as NotebookLM for deeper source work.

item.title: Google Assistant
item.description: Google Assistant is the voice assistant that ships on Android phones, Nest speakers and displays, Android Auto, Wear OS watches, and many third-party smart home devices. You wake it with a phrase or a button, then ask it to set a timer, add a calendar event, send a message, play music, or turn off the lights. It works well for short, concrete commands, and a large ecosystem of smart home brands supports it, which made it one of the more capable options for controlling a connected home.

item.title: Kagi
item.description:
Kagi takes a different business model from other search engines: users pay a subscription, and in return there are no ads, no tracking-based profiles, and no incentive to favor advertisers. Results are meant to be clean and relevant, and the company says it does not sell data. The service uses several sources, including its own index of smaller sites, and puts effort into reducing low-quality content and SEO spam.

Control is a defining feature. Users can raise, lower, or block domains, so a site that is always useless for you disappears, and lenses restrict a search to a set of sources, such as forums or academic sites. AI tools include summaries of pages and videos, answers with citations, and an assistant that gives access to multiple language models. Kagi has also launched Orion, a privacy-focused browser, and other products around the search experience.

item.title: Kimi
item.description:
Kimi first gained attention for handling very long documents. Users can upload large PDFs, books, or collections of files and ask questions, and the assistant keeps track of the whole text, which suited tasks like summarizing reports and analyzing contracts. It also searches the web, writes and reasons about code, and has agent features that carry out multi-step tasks.

Moonshot AI releases powerful models, including open-weight versions of its Kimi K2 family, which are among the larger open models and strong at coding and agentic tasks. Developers use them through Moonshot’s API or run them through third-party providers, and they are often used inside coding tools. The company competes with other Chinese labs such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Zhipu.

item.title: Le Chat
item.description:
Le Chat is Mistral’s answer to ChatGPT and Claude. The French company designed the app for general use: answering questions, writing and editing, summarizing documents, analyzing images, generating images, and running code. Fast response modes make it quick for everyday queries, and a canvas supports working on documents and code beside the chat.

Further features address more advanced needs. Deep research compiles longer reports from web sources, connectors link to services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Notion, and custom agents let users set up specialized assistants. Memory can retain preferences between chats, and mobile apps bring it to phones. The assistant uses Mistral’s own models, some of which are open-weight, and emphasizes European hosting and privacy options.

item.title: Meta AI
item.description: Meta AI is the assistant that Meta put where its users already are. In WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, and Facebook, you can mention it in a chat or open it from the search bar to ask a question, get recommendations, or generate an image. There is also a standalone app and website with fuller features, including natural voice conversations, image creation and editing, and a feed where people share what they have made.

item.title: Miro AI
item.description:
Miro provides an infinite shared canvas where teams place sticky notes, diagrams, documents, and images, and work together live or asynchronously. It’s used for brainstorming, retrospectives, user journey maps, roadmaps, and workshops, particularly for distributed teams. A large library of templates, integrations with tools such as Jira, Slack, and Google Drive, and facilitation features like timers and voting make it versatile.

AI features speed up creation and synthesis. Users can generate diagrams, flowcharts, and mind maps from a prompt, summarize and cluster hundreds of sticky notes into themes, and turn a board into a document or a prototype. Sidekicks are AI helpers with specific roles, such as a product manager or a retrospective facilitator, that give feedback and suggestions on the board. Flows connect several AI steps for repeatable processes.

item.title: Perplexity
item.description: Perplexity works more like a search engine than a chatbot. You ask a question, it searches the web in real time, and it writes a short answer with numbered citations you can click to check. That makes it good for current events, product comparisons, and fact-finding where you need to see where the information came from. Follow-up questions keep the context, and you can narrow searches to sources like academic papers or forums.

item.title: Perplexity AI
item.description:
Perplexity positions itself as an alternative to the list of links. You ask a question in natural language, it searches the web in real time, reads the pages, and writes a concise answer with citations to each source. That format is helpful for questions where you want a quick overview with a way to check the evidence, such as product comparisons, news, how-to questions, and research basics.

The experience supports continued exploration. Follow-up questions build on earlier context, and focus options narrow the search to categories such as academic sources or discussion forums. Pro Search runs more steps for complex questions, and Deep Research generates longer reports. The Comet browser brings the assistant into everyday browsing, and Spaces organize related research. Users can choose among several models in paid plans.

item.title: Phind
item.description: Phind was built for programmers who had questions that a standard search engine handled poorly. A developer could ask how to fix an error, compare libraries, or write a function, and Phind searched the web and documentation, then wrote an answer with code snippets and links to its sources. It used its own coding-focused models and later offered an IDE extension and a chat interface for follow-up questions, and it was popular as a free alternative to general chatbots.

item.title: Pi
item.description:
Pi was built to be a kind and curious conversational partner instead of a productivity tool. Its responses are short, warm, and conversational, and it often asks follow-up questions, which made it a favorite with people who wanted to talk through ideas, plans, or feelings in a low-pressure setting. It supports voice conversations with several voices, which suits casual use.

Inflection AI, founded by former DeepMind and LinkedIn leaders, launched Pi with the aim of making a personal AI. The company later saw its founders and much of its team join Microsoft, and it pivoted to licensing its models to enterprises. Pi remains online as a free consumer product at pi.ai and in apps, but active development has slowed, and the messaging integrations it once had are gone.

item.title: Poe
item.description:
Poe gives access to many AI models without separate accounts. A single app and website lets you switch between leading chatbots, image generators, and video tools, compare answers, and keep your conversations in one place. This is helpful for people who want to try different models and use whichever works best for each task.

Creators can build bots on top of models with custom prompts and knowledge, and publish them for others, with ways to earn revenue based on usage. The platform also offers an app builder and an API so developers can use Poe’s models in their projects. Group chats let multiple bots and people interact in one conversation.

item.title: Raycast AI
item.description:
Raycast puts a command bar on your keyboard. Press a hotkey, type a few letters, and you can launch apps, search files, run calculations, manage windows, paste snippets, control music, and use hundreds of extensions that connect to tools such as GitHub, Linear, Notion, and Slack. Power users value how much it can cut mouse use and context switching.

Raycast AI adds chat and commands powered by leading language models. You can ask a question, rewrite selected text, summarize a page, translate, or run custom AI commands from any app, and switch among models from different providers. AI Extensions let the assistant act through extensions, such as creating an issue or checking a calendar, and Model Context Protocol support connects it to more tools. Chats and presets are synced across devices.

item.title: Replika
item.description: Replika is one of the earliest AI companion apps. You create an avatar, choose a name and appearance, and begin chatting. Over time the AI builds a memory of your interests, relationships, and preferences, and the avatar responds in a way that reflects that history. Users talk to it about their day, vent about problems, practice conversations, or just keep company. It offers text chat, voice calls, and an augmented reality mode that places the avatar in your room.

item.title: Siri
item.description: Siri is the assistant that comes with every Apple device. You say “Hey Siri” or hold a button, then ask it to send a message, set a timer, call someone, play music, adjust a setting, or control HomeKit devices. It works across Apple’s hardware, so the same assistant is on your wrist, in your car through CarPlay, and on a smart speaker. Its biggest advantage is how deeply it ties into the system, since it can act on messages, calendars, reminders, and photos without extra setup.

item.title: Sunsama
item.description:
Sunsama is built around the idea that planning your day deliberately reduces overwhelm. Each morning, a guided ritual walks you through gathering tasks from different sources, choosing what you can realistically do, estimating the time each will take, and placing them on your calendar. The app shows your total planned hours against the day’s available time, which discourages overcommitting.

It connects to many other tools. Tasks from project managers, issue trackers, email, and Slack can be brought into your daily view without leaving Sunsama, and calendar events appear alongside them. An end-of-day shutdown ritual lets you review what you finished and move unfinished tasks forward. AI features help with suggestions for scheduling, summaries, and organizing tasks.

item.title: Todoist
item.description: Todoist is a clean, fast task manager. You add tasks by typing in plain language, like “send report every Friday at 3pm,” and it turns that into a recurring due date. Tasks can be organized into projects and sections, given priorities and labels, and viewed as a list, board, or calendar. Filters let you build views such as everything due today across all projects. It syncs across phones, computers, browsers, and email clients.

item.title: Venice AI
item.description: Venice AI builds its pitch around privacy and freedom of use. The company states it does not log or store conversations on its servers, and that chats are kept in the user’s browser, which appeals to people uneasy about their prompts being retained or used for training. It runs open-source models, so users can pick from several language models and an image generator, and the platform applies fewer content restrictions than many mainstream services.

item.title: You.com
item.description:
You.com is a search engine that mixes web results with AI-generated answers. You ask a question and receive a conversational response with links to sources, along with traditional results and apps for tasks like coding or image creation. A privacy focus has been part of its positioning, with a private mode and a commitment to not selling personal data.

The product has moved toward agents and enterprise search. Research and agent modes run multi-step investigations and produce longer reports, a custom agent builder lets people create assistants for specific tasks, and the platform lets users switch among models from different providers. For developers and businesses, You.com offers APIs that deliver live web search results formatted for AI applications, which several AI companies use to ground their answers.

item.title: Notion
item.description: Notion works as a set of building blocks. A team can create a company wiki, a project tracker with a board view, a product roadmap, a meeting notes database, and a documentation site, all in one workspace with permissions and comments. Databases are central: the same set of records can be viewed as a table, board, calendar, or timeline, and linked to other databases, which makes it possible to build custom systems without code.

item.title: Alexa AI
item.description:
Alexa popularized the smart speaker. You speak to an Echo device to play music, set timers, control lights, check weather, shop on Amazon, and ask questions. Over the years, it grew into a platform with thousands of skills from third parties and support for a huge range of smart home devices. It’s built into many speakers, TVs, cars, and appliances.

Alexa+ is the next generation. Built on large language models, including Amazon’s own Nova and models from other providers, it holds more natural conversations, understands context across a dialogue, and can handle multi-step requests such as planning an evening, booking a reservation, or coordinating a family calendar. It can act across services, remember preferences, and work with smart home devices more flexibly, and a web and app experience complements the voice interface. Some promised features arrived later than first shown.

item.title: Akiflow
item.description: Akiflow is built for people whose tasks are scattered across many apps. A task might arrive as an email, a Slack message, a Jira ticket, or an Asana item, and Akiflow collects them in a universal inbox so you can decide what to do and when. You drag tasks onto a calendar to block out time for them, which turns a long to-do list into a realistic day. Keyboard shortcuts and a command bar make it fast to use.

item.title: Anna
item.description:
Anna presents itself as an adaptive AI companion. Instead of treating every chat as new, it tries to remember what you have told it and adjusts its tone and suggestions as it learns your preferences and goals. That continuity is the main selling point of companion-style apps.

People use apps like this for conversation, motivation, planning, and reflection. They differ from task-focused assistants in that they emphasize an ongoing relationship. Mainstream assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude have also added memory, so the line between categories is blurring.

item.title: Chai
item.description:
Chai lets people talk to a huge variety of AI personalities. Users browse or search for characters, such as a friendly companion, a fantasy hero, or a fictional figure, and chat in a messaging-style interface. Creators can build their own characters by writing a short description and a first message, and they are shared with the community, which has produced a very large catalog.

The experience is aimed at entertainment and companionship. The AI maintains a persona and some memory of the conversation, and the app offers features such as voice and image options and a feed of popular bots. Free users see ads and message limits, while subscribers get faster responses and more features.

item.title: Character.ai
item.description: Character.AI lets you chat with an enormous catalog of AI personalities. Some are based on fictional characters or historical figures, many are invented by users, and you can build your own by writing a description of who the character is and how they talk. The results feel more like acting than answering questions: the characters stay in persona, remember what you have said in the conversation, and respond in a distinctive voice. Users spend long sessions on it, using it for role-play, story writing, language practice, and casual company.

item.title: ChatPlayground AI
item.description:
ChatPlayground addresses a simple question: which model is best for this task? Instead of opening several chatbots in separate tabs, a user types a prompt once and sees answers from multiple models side by side, including offerings from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and open models.

That helps with writing, coding, and research tasks where quality varies by model. Users can save conversations, keep prompts organized, and switch between models while working. For people who pay for several subscriptions, a single place can be convenient.

item.title: Choosaro
item.description:
Choosaro structures the way you decide. You list the options, such as three laptops or two job offers, then define the criteria that matter, like price, quality, or location, and assign each a weight. Scoring the options against the criteria produces a ranked result that shows which choice best fits your priorities.

The method is a weighted decision matrix, a familiar technique that makes tradeoffs explicit. Writing criteria down helps people notice what they really care about and gives teams a shared basis for discussion. AI features can suggest criteria and help fill in details.

item.title: Collate
item.description:
Collate focuses on private document work. A user opens a PDF, such as a paper, contract, or textbook, and asks questions about it or requests a summary. Because the processing runs locally on the device, the document does not need to leave the computer, which matters for sensitive files.

Typical uses include studying, reviewing research papers, and pulling key terms from long reports. Local models are smaller than cloud models, so results are good for summaries and questions about the text but may be less strong on complex reasoning, and speed depends on the hardware.

item.title: Grok
item.description: Grok is the chatbot from xAI, Elon Musk’s AI company. It is built into X, so you can ask it about a post, a trending topic, or a thread without leaving the feed, and it is also available as a separate app and at grok.com. Its main distinguishing feature is live access to posts on X, which makes it unusually quick at summarizing what people are saying about a breaking story. The tone is a little looser than other assistants, and it will answer some questions that more cautious tools decline.

item.title: Kin Personal AI
item.description:
Kin positions itself as a private personal AI. Users talk with an assistant that remembers their circumstances and offers guidance across areas of life, with specialized advisors that focus on different topics. The conversation builds a profile over time so advice reflects what the user has shared.

Privacy is the main selling point. The company states that personal data is stored locally on the device and encrypted, rather than in a central cloud, so sensitive details are less exposed. This appeals to people who want to discuss personal matters without handing data to a large platform.

item.title: Kindroid
item.description:
Kindroid lets users create a companion from scratch. You write the character’s background and personality, choose how they look using generated images, and give them a voice, and then talk by text or voice calls. The app emphasizes memory, so the character can recall details from earlier conversations, and users can adjust how the AI responds by editing the character’s profile and diary.

Other features include group chats with several characters, image generation of the character in various scenes, and selfie sharing. Users value the high level of control and the more natural conversation compared with simpler chatbots. Some use it for roleplay and storytelling, others for companionship or practicing conversation.

item.title: Littlebird
item.description:
Littlebird tries to understand what you are working on. It observes activity across apps, such as messages, meetings, documents, and web pages, and builds a memory of context. When a user asks for help, such as summarizing a project status or drafting a reply, it draws on that history.

The pitch is an assistant that does not need to be told everything each time. That convenience comes with a privacy tradeoff, since an always-on tool sees a lot of work content. Users should understand what is captured, where it is stored, and how to pause or delete it.

item.title: Microsoft Copilot
item.description: Microsoft uses the Copilot name for a family of assistants rather than one product. The consumer Copilot app and website work like other AI chatbots: you can ask questions, generate text and images, talk by voice, and have it look at your screen or camera for help with what you are doing. It is built into Windows and the Edge browser, where it can summarize pages, compare information across open tabs, and help with tasks as you browse.

item.title: Notis
item.description:
Notis works where people already chat. Users send a text or voice note to the assistant in a messaging app, and it can save notes, draft emails, set tasks, search the web, or update tools like Notion and calendars. The aim is to reduce the friction of opening several apps.

Connections to services such as Gmail, Google Calendar, and Notion let the assistant act on requests, and it keeps a memory of preferences. Voice notes are transcribed and organized.

item.title: Reclaim AI
item.description:
Reclaim is a smart scheduling assistant. You tell it your priorities, tasks with deadlines, recurring habits such as lunch or exercise, and preferred meeting hours, and it places them in your calendar. When a new meeting appears, Reclaim moves flexible items around automatically, so your calendar stays workable without constant manual rescheduling.

Several features support teams. Smart one-on-ones find times that work for both participants and adjust over time, scheduling links let others book you at times that fit your priorities, and focus time blocks protect deep work. Integrations pull tasks from tools like Asana, ClickUp, Todoist, Linear, and Jira and schedule them, and analytics show how you spend time.

item.title: Serno
item.description:
Serno gives users a single place to consult multiple models. A person asks a question once and sees how different systems respond, with differences highlighted, which can reveal uncertainty or disagreement that a single answer would hide.

This approach suits research, strategy, and decisions where one model’s blind spot could mislead. Saved conversations and comparisons make it easy to revisit reasoning, and some workflows ask models to critique each other.

item.title: Slack AI
item.description:
Slack AI addresses the problem of catching up. When you return from time off or join a busy channel, it can summarize what happened, list decisions, and highlight what needs your attention. Thread summaries cut long discussions into a few lines, and daily recaps cover channels you choose, so you can stay informed without reading every message.

AI search turns Slack into a place to ask questions. Instead of hunting for keywords, you can ask something like what the timeline is for a project, and receive an answer drawn from messages, files, and connected apps, with links to the sources. Slackbot is being reshaped as an assistant that can help draft messages, find information, and take actions, and Salesforce’s Agentforce agents can work in Slack. Huddle notes summarize audio calls.

item.title: Slashspace
item.description:
Slashspace rethinks chatting with AI as a workspace instead of a single scrolling thread. Conversations live on a canvas where users branch ideas, keep multiple threads open, and combine sources, so research does not get buried in a long chat history.

The app supports several models, lets users bring in documents and web pages, and keeps context organized. Writers and analysts use it to explore a topic from different angles and compare lines of reasoning.

item.title: TheLibrarian.io
item.description:
TheLibrarian.io puts an assistant in WhatsApp. Users message it to check their email, schedule events, create tasks, and get reminders, in natural language or voice notes. It connects to services like Gmail and Google Calendar.

The appeal is simplicity: no new interface, and the chat is available anywhere. Connecting an assistant to email and calendars requires trust, so review permissions and privacy terms.

Independent information is limited. It has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Notis, Poke, Lindy, Motion, and ChatGPT with connectors. TheLibrarian.io suits people who want to manage tasks through WhatsApp.

item.title: Wispr Flow
item.description:
Wispr Flow turns speech into polished text. A user presses a key, talks, and the cleaned-up text appears wherever the cursor is. The AI removes filler words, fixes false starts, handles punctuation, and adjusts tone to the app, so messages and documents read as if typed.

It supports many languages, custom vocabulary for names and terms, and commands for editing by voice. Writers, developers, and professionals use it to speed up emails, notes, and prompts for AI tools.

item.title: ZeroTwo
item.description:
ZeroTwo is a multi-model chat workspace. A user picks a model for each conversation or compares several, and keeps history, files, and prompts in one place. It supports web search, image generation, and document analysis.

For people who use several AI products, a combined interface can simplify life and cost. Pricing is typically a single subscription instead of many.

Access to the newest features of each provider may lag the official apps. ZeroTwo has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Poe, TypingMind, ChatHub, OpenRouter’s chat, and Open WebUI. ZeroTwo suits power users who work across models.
